chapters.title: From Zero to Hello
chapters.scope: Start from nothing: a program is a list of instructions run in order, and the computer does exactly what is written, never what you meant. Source code is just text in a `.go` file; a compiler translates that text into a binary (an executable file) the machine can run, which is why Go is called compiled. Name the two moments: compile time (the translator's desk, where compile errors are caught) and run time (the kitchen, where runtime panics happen). Output means what the program prints; standard output vs error output are two separate streams. Classic wrong idea: a `.go` file runs directly like a document. Then the tools: download Go from go.dev, PATH, opening a terminal, the current directory, `cd`, `mkdir`, `ls`/`dir`, `go version` (shows `go version go1.27.3 linux/amd64`), `go env`, `go help`, the Go Playground as a zero-install option, and that GOTOOLCHAIN=auto may download a newer toolchain. Mistakes: running `go` before it is on PATH (the shell, not Go, says command not found; wording varies by shell), `cd hello` before `mkdir hello`, and `go run .` outside a module: `go: go.mod file not found in current directory or any parent directory; see 'go help modules'`. Then the smallest module: `go mod init example/hello` prints `go: creating new go.mod: module example/hello`, and the go.mod it writes (module line and `go 1.27.3`). Hello World anatomy line by line: `package main`, `import "fmt"`, `func main()`, braces, statements, string literal in double quotes, `fmt.Println`, comments `//` and `/* */`, automatic semicolons; `go run .`, `go build` (success prints nothing) and running the binary. First errors read like a detective (file:line:column first): opening brace on its own line `./main.go:6:1: syntax error: unexpected semicolon or newline before {`; code outside a function `./main.go:3:1: syntax error: non-declaration statement outside function body`; missing package line `main.go:1:1: expected 'package', found 'import'`; missing func main `runtime.main_main·f: function main is undeclared in the main package`; unused import `./main.go:5:2: "os" imported and not used`.

Map: write -> compile -> run -> output, with the two error exits (translator's desk = compile error, kitchen = panic) drawn as side roads. chapters.title: Squiggles and Sums
chapters.scope: Tools first: VS Code with the Go extension (gopls), red squiggles vs real compile errors, format-on-save; `gofmt -l` lists unformatted files, `gofmt -d` shows the diff (it turns `func  X( )int{return 1}` into `func X() int { return 1 }`) and only changes spacing, never behavior; `go vet` is a proof-reader for code that compiles but is suspicious. Anatomy of an error: the `# example/pkg` header line, then `file:line:column: message` read like a street address (file, house number, door); fix the first error first because later ones are often caused by it; vet messages have no header line (example to show: `main.go:7:14: fmt.Printf format %d has arg name of wrong type string`, only as 'vet catches this' preview; Printf itself is ch4). Then values: integer literals, float literals, string literals, `true`/`false`; operators `+ - * / %`; integer division truncates (`7/2` is `3`, `7.0/2` is `3.5`); `%` gives the leftover and its sign follows the dividend (`7%3` is `1`, `-7%3` is `-1`); precedence and parentheses; `fmt.Println` with several arguments adds spaces; string concatenation with `+`; escape `\n`. Mistakes with real messages: adding a string and an int `invalid operation: "age: " + age (mismatched types untyped string and int)` (show with a literal-only version so it needs no variables, or keep it for ch3), constant division by zero `invalid operation: division by zero`; ignoring the line/column; fixing the last error first.

chapters.title: Boxes and Stone
chapters.scope: Variables as labelled boxes: `var x int` builds a box that already holds its zero value, `var x = 5` lets Go infer the type, `x := 5` builds and fills in one step, `=` replaces the contents of an existing box; `=` vs `:=`. Zero values: 0, 0.0, "", false, nil (name only). Multiple assignment and the swap `a, b = b, a`. Naming rules and MixedCaps; block scope (a name lives inside its braces); unused variables are errors; the blank identifier `_`. Mistakes with real messages: `./main.go:4:2: declared and not used: x`, `./main.go:7:4: no new variables on left side of :=`, `./main.go:6:14: undefined: total`, and `:=` at package level giving the non-declaration-statement syntax error from ch1. Then constants: `const`, carved in stone vs a whiteboard variable; constants cannot change (assigning to one is a compile error); typed vs untyped constants; constant expressions are computed at compile time (untyped numeric constants can be huge: `const big = 1 << 100; fmt.Println(big >> 98)`); constant overflow is caught by the compiler `./main.go:4:16: cannot use 300 (untyped int constant) as uint8 value in variable declaration (overflows)`; constant float to int `cannot convert 3.99 (untyped float constant) to type int`; a first look at `iota` (counting 0, 1, 2 in a const block) with full enums deferred. Choice practice: const or var for days in a week.

chapters.title: Odometers and Blanks
chapters.scope: Number types in depth: int vs int8/16/32/64, the uint family, byte = uint8, rune = int32 (name only), float32/float64, complex mentioned only; explicit conversion `T(x)` is the funnel between different-sized jars; float to int truncates; integer overflow wraps silently at run time (no undefined behavior): `math.MaxInt64` plus one prints `-9223372036854775808`, uint 0 minus one prints `18446744073709551615`, uint8 255 plus one prints `0`; float imprecision: variables `x, y := 0.1, 0.2; x+y` prints `0.30000000000000004` but the constant `0.1 + 0.2` prints `0.3` (constants are exact, links back to ch3); the `math` package and `math.MaxInt64`; choosing a type (age, bank balance in cents). Mistakes: `invalid operation: a + b (mismatched types int and float64)`, `cannot use n (variable of type int) as float64 value in argument to math.Sqrt`, and the fix `float64(total) / float64(count)`. Then printing: `Print`, `Println`, `Printf`, `Sprintf`, `Errorf` named as a preview; verbs `%v %+v %#v %T %d %s %q %f %.2f %x %t %p` (show %p only as 'changes every run'); width and padding `%5d %-5d %08.3f`; `\n` in Printf. Classic mistakes and real output: forgetting `\n` so lines run together; wrong verb still runs and prints `%!d(string=Ana)`; too few args prints `Ana %!s(MISSING)`; too many prints `1%!(EXTRA int=2)`; `go vet` flags all of these (back to ch2's proof-reader). The struct-printing example (`%v | %+v | %#v | %T` giving `{Ana 30} | {Name:Ana Age:30} | main.P{Name:"Ana", Age:30} | main.P`) and how nil slices/maps/errors print (`[] map[] <nil> <nil>`) belong in ch12 when structs and maps exist; here use numbers, strings and bools only.

chapters.title: Forks and Doors
chapters.scope: Booleans: `bool`, comparison `== != < <= > >=`, logic `&&`, `||`, `!`, short-circuit evaluation (prove it with a function that prints when called), comparing strings byte-wise and case-sensitive (`"Apple" < "apple"` does not ignore case), and no truthiness: an int is not a bool (`if x` with an int is a compile error, non-boolean condition), comparing int and float needs a conversion (mismatched types). Then if/else: `if cond {}`, `else`, `else if` chains where order matters (>=90 before >=80 in a grade calculator), braces are mandatory and parentheses are not needed, the short statement `if v := f(); v > 0 {}` and its scope (using v after the if is undefined), early return previewed. Mistakes: `if x = 5 {` gives `syntax error: cannot use assignment x = 5 as value`; `=` vs `==`; a function whose if has no final return gives `./main.go:7:1: missing return` (show only if functions are simple enough; otherwise defer to ch7). Then switch: expression switch, several values per case `case "sat", "sun":`, `default`, no automatic fallthrough (unlike what some expect), the `fallthrough` keyword, tagless `switch {}` as a tidy if-chain, switch with an init statement, `break` inside switch exits only the switch. Mistakes: `duplicate case 1 (constant of type int) in expression switch` with its `previous case` detail line; `cannot fallthrough final case in switch`; choosing switch vs if-chain.
chapters.not_yet: Loops, so the 'break inside switch inside a loop prints 0, 1, 2' trap waits for ch6; functions and `missing return` in depth (ch7); type switches (ch14).

chapters.title: Laps and Egg Cartons
chapters.scope: for loops, four ways: three-part `for i := 0; i < n; i++`, condition-only (Go's while), infinite `for {}` with `break`, and `for i := range 10` (Go 1.22+); `continue` skips the rest of this lap, `break` leaves the stadium, labels with `break outer` name which loop to leave; nested loops (multiplication table); `i++` is a statement, not an expression; each iteration gets a fresh variable since Go 1.22 (state it; the closure proof is ch17); `for i, v := range` previewed with arrays below. Classic mistakes: off-by-one `i <= len(s)` prints a, b, c then `panic: runtime error: index out of range [3] with length 3`; `continue is not in a loop`; range over int with an old go.mod `cannot range over 3 (untyped int constant): requires go1.22 or later (-lang was set to go1.21; check go.mod)`; the switch trap from ch5: `break` inside a switch inside a loop does not stop the loop (prints 0, 1, 2). FizzBuzz as the classic. Then arrays: `[3]int`, `[...]int{1,2,3}`, length is part of the type, indexing from 0, `len`, ranging over an array, arrays are values so assignment copies (copy-then-modify shows the original unchanged), comparing arrays with `==`, multi-dimensional arrays, and why slices are used more. Mistake: constant out-of-range index caught by the compiler `invalid argument: index 5 out of bounds [0:3]`, while a variable index panics at run time.

chapters.title: Machines and Mail Slots
chapters.scope: Functions as vending machines: `func name(a int, b int) int`, shared parameter types `a, b int`, return values, multiple return values, named results and naked return (and why to avoid long ones), the documentation comment above a function, local scope, `_` to ignore a result, call by value (the machine works on its own copy of your coins: changing a parameter does not change the caller's int), functions as the main tool for breaking a long main into steps. Mistakes with real messages: `too many return values` / `not enough return values` followed by the tab-indented `have (number)` and `want (int, error)` lines; `missing return` when one branch forgets to return. (The struct version of call-by-value, `move(a)` printing `{1 2}`, waits for ch12-13.) Then input, which always arrives as text through a mail slot: `fmt.Scan` and `fmt.Scanln` with `&name` explained only as 'give Scan the address of your box' (pointers are ch13), `bufio.NewScanner(os.Stdin)` with `scanner.Scan()` and `scanner.Text()`, `os.Args` and `os.Args[1:]`, `strings.TrimSpace`, `strconv.Atoi` (the clerk who reads the paper and fills a number box or hands back a complaint slip), `strconv.Itoa`, `strconv.ParseFloat`. Here functions returning two values pay off: `n, err := strconv.Atoi(s)`. Classic mistakes and real output: `fmt.Scanln(&name)` with input "Ada Lovelace" stores only `Ada`; `n := strconv.Atoi(s)` gives `assignment mismatch: 1 variable but strconv.Atoi returns 2 values`; `strconv.Atoi("abc")` error text `strconv.Atoi: parsing "abc": invalid syntax`; too big `strconv.Atoi: parsing "99999999999999999999": value out of range`; scanning letters into an int leaves `n` at `0` with err `expected integer`. Print the error here; the full check-and-return habit is ch8.

chapters.title: Receipts and Footprints
chapters.scope: Errors as values, the receipt that comes with every delivery: functions return `(value, error)`, `nil` means no error, check immediately with `if err != nil`, return early (`return 0, err`), make your own with `errors.New` and `fmt.Errorf` (no `%w` yet), print an error, the value is useless (a zero value) when err != nil, and do not panic on bad input; choose return-an-error vs print-and-continue. Classic mistakes: ignoring err and using the zero value (`fmt.Scan` example prints `0 expected integer`); dropping an error result silently, e.g. `os.Remove("nothing-here")` compiles and runs with no output; `os.Open` failure text `open nofile.txt: no such file or directory` (shown as an error value only; files proper are ch14). chapters.title: Windows on a Shelf

Benchmark timings vary: only allocs/op and B/op from `-benchmem` (or `testing.AllocsPerRun` printed by a program) may be answers; ns/op is .nondet and must be masked. pprof output is machine-dependent: notebook transcript only. Spot-the-bug snippets must each be a real captured program (compile error or real wrong output).
